Cross-modality Person Re-identification¶

COMP9444 Group Project · Group "KeyError: 'GroupName'" · Visible–infrared retrieval on SYSU-MM01

We study infrared-to-visible person retrieval with the Progressive Modality-shared Transformer (PMT) as the baseline. We test two extensions of our own design, a smooth grey-to-colour transition (S) and auxiliary local supervision (L), and channel augmentation (CA) taken from CAJ [4]. All are compared under one data split, sampler and evaluator. The final stage retrains PMT and the candidate chosen on validation (PMT + CA) on 395 identities and evaluates them once on the test split.

Summary of findings¶

  • Baselines (validation, three seeds). PMT (M0) reaches 34.6 mAP / 32.2 Rank-1. It is above a plain ViT (V0) and the CNN baseline AGW on all 30 seed–gallery pairs, and 0.8 mAP above our corrected CAJ. CAJ with the authors' code collapsed during training; a one-line correction restored it (Section 5.3).

1. Introduction, Motivation and Problem Statement¶

Visible–infrared person re-identification matches an infrared query image to visible-light images of the same person across cameras. Differences in spectrum, lighting, pose and occlusion make appearance matching difficult. The objective is to learn features that preserve identity across modalities and rank matching gallery images highly, including for identities unseen during training.

We use the Progressive Modality-shared Transformer (PMT) [1] as our baseline. We investigate whether a smoother grey-to-colour transition and auxiliary local supervision improve retrieval, individually and together, and whether channel augmentation from a CNN method transfers to PMT. Performance is assessed with mAP, mINP and Rank-1/5/10/20 on identity-disjoint evaluation data.

Research questions:

  • RQ1. Does a smooth greyscale transition improve retrieval and stability around the stage switch, compared with PMT's direct switch?
  • RQ2. Can local patch-feature supervision complement the global feature, especially when part of the body is missing?
  • RQ3. Are the two extensions complementary, and is any gain worth its extra cost?

2. Data Sources¶

We use SYSU-MM01, supplied through the course-linked Kaggle mirror, with the official identity splits [2]. Cameras 1, 2, 4 and 5 capture RGB images; cameras 3 and 6 capture infrared images.

The dataset contains 45,863 images: 30,071 RGB and 15,792 IR. Development uses 296 training identities and 99 validation identities; 96 test identities are reserved for final evaluation. The downloaded directories contain 22 additional identities absent from the official split lists. Their 1,118 images are excluded.

3. Exploratory Analysis of Data¶

3.1 Data balance and integrity¶

The training split has 20,284 RGB images and 9,929 IR images, approximately a 2:1 imbalance. We therefore sample equally from both modalities and balance identities within each training batch. All training identities have images in both modalities. The audit found no unreadable images, overlapping official identity splits or duplicate files shared across splits.

Camera-level image counts also vary, as shown below. These counts describe dataset coverage; they do not establish how difficult each camera is for retrieval.

4. Models and Methods¶

All models in this project share the data split, the identity-balanced sampler and the evaluator. The figure gives an overview of PMT and the optional modules; each module is switched on by configuration only, so every comparison differs from M0 in the target factor alone.

Overview: PMT (grey boxes) and the optional modules S, CA and L (coloured), with the runs that enable each.

4.1 PMT (M0)¶

PMT is the main method of this project: both proposed extensions are built on it, and it is referred to as M0 in the experiments. We implement PMT following Lu et al. [1] and the pinned author PyTorch implementation. The shared ViT-B/16 has 12 blocks, 12 attention heads and 768-dimensional features. A 16×16 patch projection with stride 12 produces a 21×10 patch grid from 256×128 images. The CLS feature feeds a BN neck and an identity classifier. Metric losses use the pre-BN feature; retrieval uses the L2-normalised, post-BN global feature.

Training has two stages. Epochs 1–6 use greyscale RGB and IR inputs with identity classification and separate within-modality hard-triplet losses. Epochs 7–24 restore colour RGB and use joint hard-triplet, modality discrepancy (MSEL) and centre-based (DCL) losses:

$$L_1=L_{ID}^{R}+L_{ID}^{I}+L_{tri}^{R}+L_{tri}^{I}.$$ $$L_2=L_{ID}^{R}+L_{ID}^{I}+L_{tri}^{all}+0.5L_{MSEL}+0.5L_{DCL}.$$

MSEL aligns within- and cross-modality positive distances; DCL encourages identity-centred separation. We retain the stage-2 ID term as in the author's PyTorch code. PMT and its losses are prior work; our contribution here is the implementation and experiment. The augmentation recipe includes the author's random-erasing implementation. Source attribution and implementation differences are recorded in ATTRIBUTION.md and docs/baseline.md.

PMT (M0): shared ViT-B/16 with overlapping patches, BN neck and the two-stage objective.

Core implementation. The cells below are excerpts of src/model.py and src/losses.py (the ViT blocks themselves are standard and omitted). Metric losses use the pre-BN CLS feature in FP32; the BN-neck output feeds the classifier and, after L2 normalisation, retrieval. A batch holds P identities × K images of RGB followed by the same identities in IR, which MSEL and DCL rely on.

In [4]:
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn import functional as F


class PMT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes, model_config=None, pretrained=None):
        super().__init__()
        cfg = model_config or {}
        dim = cfg.get("global_feature_dim", 768)
        self.base = VisionTransformer(image_size=cfg.get("image_size", (256, 128)),
            patch_size=cfg.get("patch_size", 16), patch_stride=cfg.get("patch_stride", 12),
            dim=dim, depth=cfg.get("depth", 12), heads=cfg.get("heads", 12),
            dropout=cfg.get("dropout", .03), attention_dropout=cfg.get("attention_dropout", 0.),
            drop_path=cfg.get("drop_path", .1), activation_checkpointing=cfg.get("activation_checkpointing", False))
        self.bottleneck = nn.BatchNorm1d(dim)
        self.bottleneck.bias.requires_grad_(False)
        self.classifier = nn.Linear(dim, num_classes, bias=False)
        nn.init.normal_(self.classifier.weight, std=.001)
        if pretrained is not None:
            self.base.load_pretrained(pretrained)

    def forward(self, images):
        global_feature, patches, grid = self.base(images)
        bn_feature = self.bottleneck(global_feature)
        return {"global_feature": global_feature, "global_logits": self.classifier(bn_feature),
                "retrieval_feature": F.normalize(bn_feature, dim=1),
                "patch_features": patches, "patch_grid": grid,
                "local_features": None, "local_logits": None}
In [5]:
def distances(x, y):
    # FP32 even when the backbone uses autocast: avoid half-precision cancellation.
    x, y = x.float(), y.float()
    return (x.square().sum(1)[:, None] + y.square().sum(1)[None, :] - 2 * x @ y.T).clamp_min(1e-12).sqrt()


def validate_layout(labels, k):
    if k < 2 or labels.ndim != 1 or len(labels) % (2 * k):
        raise ValueError("Expected balanced 2PK labels with K >= 2")
    a, b = labels.chunk(2)
    blocks = a.reshape(-1, k)
    if (not torch.equal(a, b) or not torch.all(blocks == blocks[:, :1])
            or len(torch.unique(blocks[:, 0])) != len(blocks) or len(blocks) < 2):
        raise ValueError("Expected distinct P >= 2 identities, contiguous K samples, RGB then IR")


def hard_triplet(features, labels, margin=.1):
    d = distances(features, features)
    same = labels[:, None] == labels[None, :]
    positives = same & ~torch.eye(len(labels), dtype=torch.bool, device=labels.device)
    if not positives.any(1).all() or not (~same).any(1).all():
        raise ValueError("Triplet requires a non-self positive and a negative per anchor")
    hardest_positive = d.masked_fill(~positives, -torch.inf).max(1).values
    hardest_negative = d.masked_fill(same, torch.inf).min(1).values
    return F.relu(hardest_positive - hardest_negative + margin).mean()


def msel(features, labels, k):
    validate_layout(labels, k)
    a, b = features.chunk(2)
    target = labels[:len(a)]
    same = target[:, None] == target[None, :]
    nonself = same & ~torch.eye(len(a), dtype=torch.bool, device=labels.device)
    intra_a = (distances(a, a) * nonself).sum(1) / (k - 1)
    intra_b = (distances(b, b) * nonself).sum(1) / (k - 1)
    cross = distances(a, b)
    cross_a = (cross * same).sum(1) / k
    cross_b = (cross.T * same).sum(1) / k
    return ((cross_a - intra_a).square().mean() + (cross_b - intra_b).square().mean()) / 2


def dcl(features, labels, k):
    validate_layout(labels, k)
    identities = labels[:len(labels) // 2:k]
    same = identities[:, None] == labels[None, :]
    centers = torch.stack([features[labels == identity].mean(0) for identity in identities])
    d = distances(centers, features)
    negatives = d[~same].reshape(len(identities), -1)
    selected = (negatives < negatives.mean(1, keepdim=True)) & (negatives > 1e-6)
    # Equal distances yield no strictly-below-mean negatives in upstream code.
    # Fall back to all negatives for that center rather than returning NaN.
    selected = torch.where(selected.any(1, keepdim=True), selected, torch.ones_like(selected))
    negative_mean = ((negatives * selected).sum(1) / selected.sum(1)).mean()
    positive = d[same]
    positive = positive[positive > 1e-6]
    positive_mean = positive.mean() if positive.numel() else d.sum() * 0
    return positive_mean / negative_mean.clamp_min(1e-6)


class PMTLoss(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, k=4, margin=.1, msel_weight=.5, dcl_weight=.5):
        super().__init__()
        self.k, self.margin = k, margin
        self.msel_weight, self.dcl_weight = msel_weight, dcl_weight

    def forward(self, output, labels, stage):
        if stage not in (1, 2, "V0"):
            raise ValueError("stage must be 1, 2 or V0")
        validate_layout(labels, self.k)
        features, logits = output["global_feature"].float(), output["global_logits"].float()
        a, b = logits.chunk(2)
        la, lb = labels.chunk(2)
        identity = F.cross_entropy(a, la) + F.cross_entropy(b, lb)
        zero = features.sum() * 0
        if stage == 1:
            fa, fb = features.chunk(2)
            triplet = hard_triplet(fa, la, self.margin) + hard_triplet(fb, lb, self.margin)
        else:
            triplet = hard_triplet(features, labels, self.margin)
        modality = msel(features, labels, self.k) if stage == 2 else zero
        center = dcl(features, labels, self.k) if stage == 2 else zero
        terms = {"id": identity, "triplet": triplet, "msel": modality, "dcl": center,
                 "weighted_msel": self.msel_weight * modality, "weighted_dcl": self.dcl_weight * center}
        terms["total"] = identity + triplet + terms["weighted_msel"] + terms["weighted_dcl"]
        return terms

4.2 Comparison baselines¶

We compare M0 with three baselines trained on the same 296 identities, with the same identity-balanced sampler and evaluator, each with training seeds 17, 42 and 2026 (CAJ with the authors' code: seed 17 only).

  • V0 is M0 without PMT's components: the same ViT-B/16 trained for 24 epochs with identity and global hard-triplet losses only, without the greyscale stage, MSEL or DCL. It measures what those components add.
  • AGW [3] is a two-stream ResNet-50 with non-local blocks and GeM pooling, trained with identity and weighted regularised triplet (WRT) losses. It is a widely used CNN baseline for this task.
  • CAJ [4] extends AGW with channel augmentation (a second RGB view with one colour channel copied to all three; random channel copying or greyscale for IR) and a squared-difference triplet loss (ADP). It tests whether simple colour augmentation already gives the benefit that the smooth-transition extension targets.

AGW and CAJ were ported from the authors' code at a pinned commit [3] and keep the authors' training settings (Section 4.3). CAJ collapsed with that code; we also report a corrected CAJ that changes only the hard-negative weighting (Section 5.3). The authors trained on 395 identities; we use 296 so that validation identities are never seen in training.

4.6 Preprocessing and training settings¶

Each model keeps the preprocessing and optimisation settings of its original implementation; only the data split, sampler and evaluator are shared. All images are normalised using ImageNet statistics, and evaluation uses resize and normalisation only.

Setting V0 / M0 (ViT-B/16) AGW / CAJ (ResNet-50)
Initialisation Author-linked ImageNet ViT-B/16 weights ImageNet ResNet-50 weights; last-stage stride 1
Input size 256×128 288×144
Training augmentation Horizontal flip, random erasing; IR also colour jitter or Gaussian blur Pad and random crop, horizontal flip; CAJ adds channel augmentation and random erasing (p = 0.5)
Batch 8 identities × 4 images × 2 modalities = 64 Same sampler: 64 images; CAJ 96 (two RGB views)
Training length 24 epochs; M0's first 6 in stage 1 AGW 81 epochs; CAJ 100 epochs
Optimiser AdamW; weight decay 0.0001 SGD, Nesterov momentum 0.9; weight decay 0.0005
Learning rate Base 0.0003; half rate for patch projection and transformer blocks Base 0.1; ×0.1 for the backbone
Schedule 3-epoch warmup, cosine decay; minimum LR 0.000003 10-epoch linear warmup; ×0.1 at epochs 20 and 50
Metric loss Hard triplet, margin 0.1 AGW: WRT; CAJ: ADP (both soft-margin, no fixed margin)
Precision Mixed precision Full precision
Training seed and device 17; NVIDIA L40S 17; NVIDIA L40S

4.4 Proposed extensions¶

The smooth-transition extension gradually reduces the probability of greyscale RGB after stage 1. The local-supervision extension adds auxiliary identity losses on horizontal feature regions. The planned M0–M3 comparison varies these two factors while keeping the backbone and global retrieval feature fixed. These extensions have not yet been evaluated.

4.5 Retrieval protocol¶

Development evaluation uses IR→RGB all-search, single-shot retrieval on the internal validation split (99 identities). Ten fixed gallery draws (seeds 0–9) are selected from the RGB candidate pool following the author's sampling procedure, and every model is scored on the same ten galleries. Cam2 gallery images are excluded for cam3 queries, following the SYSU protocol, and CMC is computed at identity level. Features are taken after the BN neck, L2-normalised and ranked by cosine similarity, without flip augmentation or re-ranking. We report mAP, mINP and Rank-k, averaged over the ten galleries. The evaluator was checked against hand-computed cases and against the author's evaluation code.

In this split, IR queries come only from camera 3 and RGB candidates only from cameras 4 and 5. Validation scores are therefore not comparable with published SYSU-MM01 test results.

The extensions (S, L, CA, band erasing) use M0's column unchanged, apart from their own configuration keys. The final stage (Section 4.8) also keeps every M0 setting, including 24 epochs, and only changes the training identities and the evaluation split.

4.8 Final stage: 395 training identities and one test evaluation¶

Model selection uses only the internal validation split. Once a candidate was fixed, the training and validation identities (296 + 99 = 395) were merged, and both M0 and the candidate were retrained from the same ImageNet initialisation with seeds 17, 42 and 2026. Training identities, the evaluation split and the step count change; every other setting is identical to development, including 24 epochs and taking the last checkpoint. The test split was not used to choose epochs, configurations or the candidate.

The candidate changed during the project, and we report the order of events. At the configuration freeze on 8 November the candidate was the local-supervision configuration L3_B050. Channel augmentation was added after the freeze, with a decision rule written before its results: replace the candidate if M0_CA is above M0 in mean validation mAP and in the same direction on every seed. M0_CA met that rule (Section 5.6), so the final stage compares M0 and M0_CA. Channel augmentation comes from CAJ [4] and is not our method.

Leakage between stages is prevented in code rather than by convention:

  • Development configurations must train on train and evaluate on val; final configurations must train on train + val (395 identities) and evaluate on test. The label map is rebuilt from the configured splits, and training stops if the identity count differs from the configuration.
  • Feature export only accepts a checkpoint's own evaluation split: a development checkpoint cannot export test features, and a final checkpoint cannot export validation features, since it was trained on them.

The export check, from src/export_features.py:

def resolve_split(cfg, requested=None):
    """Split to export for a checkpoint: its configured evaluation split.

    Development checkpoints export val only; final (train+val) checkpoints export test only.
    The test split is therefore never touched by a development model, and a final model is never
    evaluated on identities it was trained on.
    """
    split = requested or cfg["data"]["evaluation_split"]
    if split in train_splits(cfg):
        raise ValueError(f"Refusing to export {split}: this checkpoint was trained on {train_splits(cfg)}")
    if split != cfg["data"]["evaluation_split"]:
        raise ValueError(f"Refusing to export {split}: this checkpoint's evaluation split is "
                         f"{cfg['data']['evaluation_split']} (test is reserved for final-stage checkpoints)")
    return split

5. Results¶

5.1 Baseline training¶

The M0 baseline completed 24 epochs on the 296-identity training split using seed 17. The table shows mean training losses at the start and end of each stage; each row averages 633 batches. MSEL and DCL are shown before applying their 0.5 weights.

In [7]:
selected_epochs = {1, 6, 7, 24}
show_table(["Epoch", "Stage", "ID", "Triplet", "MSEL", "DCL", "Total"], [
    [row["epoch"], row["stage"], *[f"{row[key]:.4f}" for key in ["id","triplet","msel","dcl","total"]]]
    for row in measurements["epochs"] if row["epoch"] in selected_epochs])
Epoch Stage ID Triplet MSEL DCL Total
1 1 9.8951 2.4338 0.0000 0.0000 12.3289
6 1 0.5656 0.0967 0.0000 0.0000 0.6623
7 2 0.4695 0.1525 0.2096 0.6007 1.0271
24 2 0.0557 0.0183 0.0283 0.3903 0.2832

Training loss decreases within both stages: from 12.3289 to 0.6623 in stage 1 and from 1.0271 to 0.2832 in stage 2. The objective and RGB input change at epoch 7, so the boundary values are not directly comparable. These measurements describe training fit; retrieval performance must be established separately.

# All 24 epochs of the same run (mean of 633 batches per epoch).
epochs = measurements["epochs"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
for key, label in [("total", "total"), ("id", "ID"), ("triplet", "triplet"), ("msel", "MSEL"), ("dcl", "DCL")]:
    shown = [e for e in epochs if key not in ("msel", "dcl") or e["stage"] == 2]   # MSEL/DCL are off in stage 1
    ax.plot([e["epoch"] for e in shown], [e[key] for e in shown], marker="o", ms=3, label=label)
ax.axvline(6.5, color="grey", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.text(6.7, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9, "stage 2", color="grey")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("mean loss (log scale)")
ax.set_title("M0 training losses, seed 17"); ax.legend(ncol=5, fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

5.2 Baseline retrieval performance¶

Every model was trained with three seeds (17, 42, 2026) on an NVIDIA L40S and scored on the same ten fixed validation galleries. A short pilot of each new model was evaluated before its full run, to confirm that it learns before committing GPU time.

In [9]:

pct = lambda value: f"{100 * value:.1f}"

def seed_stats(name, metric):
    values = 100 * np.array([run[metric] for run in val[name]])
    return values.mean(), (values.std(ddof=1) if len(values) > 1 else float("nan"))

def mean_sd(name, metric):
    mean, sd = seed_stats(name, metric)
    return f"{mean:.1f}" if np.isnan(sd) else f"{mean:.1f} ± {sd:.1f}"

baselines = ["V0", "M0", "AGW", "CAJ", "CAJ_fix"]

            "Params (M)", "GFLOPs / image", "GPU hours (seed 17)"], [
    [labels[n], resources[n]["backbone"], resources[n]["input"], resources[n]["epochs"], len(val[n]),
     mean_sd(n, "mAP"), mean_sd(n, "mINP"), mean_sd(n, "rank1"),
     *[f"{seed_stats(n, m)[0]:.1f}" for m in ("rank5", "rank10", "rank20")],
     resources[n]["params_m"], resources[n]["gflops"], resources[n]["gpu_hours"]]
    for n in baselines])

GPU hours are the total L40S job wall time of the seed-17 run, including the pilot and feature export. † CAJ collapsed during training with the authors' code (Section 5.3), so its row is not a valid baseline result and was not repeated. ‡ Our correction of the hard-negative weighting; all other code and settings are the authors' (Section 5.3).

# Paired differences on the same galleries: 3 seeds × 10 galleries = 30 pairs (percentage points).
def paired(a, b, metric):
    return 100 * (np.array([r[f"g_{metric}"] for r in val[a]]) - np.array([r[f"g_{metric}"] for r in val[b]]))

rows = []
for a, b in (("V0", "M0"), ("AGW", "M0"), ("CAJ_fix", "M0"), ("CAJ_fix", "AGW")):
    for metric, label in (("mAP", "mAP"), ("rank1", "Rank-1")):
        diff = paired(a, b, metric)
        rows.append([f"{labels[a]} − {b}", label, f"{diff.mean() + 0.0:+.2f}",
                     " / ".join(f"{d:+.2f}" for d in diff.mean(axis=1)), f"{(diff > 0).sum()} / {diff.size}"])
show_table(["Comparison (A − B)", "Metric", "Mean", "Per seed (17 / 42 / 2026)", "Pairs where A is higher"], rows)

  • PMT components (M0 vs V0). M0 is 2.0 mAP and 4.1 Rank-1 points above V0 and higher on all 30 seed–gallery pairs, on every seed. The greyscale stage, MSEL and DCL therefore give a consistent gain over a plain ViT with the same backbone and schedule. mINP is level (24.4 vs 24.2), so the gain is in the first ranks rather than in the hardest matches.
  • Transformer PMT vs CNN baseline (M0 vs AGW). M0 is 3.9 mAP and 5.3 Rank-1 points above AGW on all 30 pairs, with about 3.6 times the parameters and computation. Backbone, input size, optimiser and losses all differ, so the gap cannot be attributed to the backbone alone.
  • Corrected CAJ vs M0. With seed 17 alone the two were level in mAP; over three seeds the corrected CAJ is 0.8 mAP below M0 (higher on 12 of 30 pairs) and level in Rank-1 (+0.02, 16 of 30). Its seed spread is the widest of the four valid baselines (Rank-1 SD 1.2), so the single-seed tie was partly chance. It reaches close to M0 with a ResNet-50 at about a quarter of the computation, but with 100 epochs and about 3.6 times M0's GPU time.
  • Corrected CAJ vs AGW. The corrected CAJ is 3.1 mAP and 5.3 Rank-1 points above AGW (29 of 30 pairs), in line with the published ordering. The gap combines channel augmentation, random erasing, the ADP loss, a larger batch, more epochs and the corrected weighting, so it is not the effect of channel augmentation alone; Section 5.6 isolates channel augmentation on PMT.
  • CAJ with the authors' code is about 20 points below AGW because of the training collapse described below.

5.3 CAJ training collapse and correction¶

With the authors' code, CAJ did not train stably on our split. The table shows per-epoch means for CAJ with the authors' code and with the corrected weighting, with AGW's training identity accuracy for reference.

For the first five epochs the ADP loss sat at its clamp value of 88, where its gradient is zero, so only the identity loss was learning. During epoch 6 the ADP term left the clamp and produced large gradients. By epoch 7, training identity accuracy had fallen from 0.85 to 0.03, close to chance (1/296). ADP settled near ln 2 ≈ 0.69, meaning the positive and negative distances had become equal: the features had collapsed. The model relearned the training identities (98% accuracy by epoch 100) but reached only 7.0% Rank-1 on validation, below its own 2-epoch pilot (11.8%).

The cause lies in the hard-sample weighting that AGW and CAJ share. When computing softmax weights over negatives, the code takes the maximum over a row that still contains masked-out zeros. With pre-BN features of norm about 50, every negative weight underflows, so the closest-negative distance evaluates to about 0. ADP then only pulls positives together, and nothing pushes different identities apart. AGW uses the same weighting, but its WRT loss has bounded gradients, and it trained normally. Taking the maximum over valid entries only restores real negative distances (about 26 at initialisation, instead of 0).

We retrained CAJ with only this change (masked_max in src/agw.py, configuration CAJ_fix); data, augmentation, losses, schedule and seed are unchanged. A 10-epoch pilot passed the epoch-6 point where the original run collapsed and reached 21.1% Rank-1, so the run was continued to 100 epochs. The ADP loss now starts at 1.65 rather than the clamp value and decreases steadily, training identity accuracy rises without a drop, and no loss value was non-finite. The final model reaches 34.4% mAP and 33.1% Rank-1. Because the code was changed, this row is our corrected implementation of CAJ, not a reproduction of the authors' code.

The weighting function from src/agw.py, with the upstream behaviour and our correction behind one flag:

In [13]:
def pairwise_distance(x):
    square = x.pow(2).sum(1, keepdim=True)
    return (square + square.t() - 2 * x @ x.t()).clamp(min=1e-12).sqrt()


def softmax_weights(dist, mask, masked_max=False):
    """Upstream takes the row max over dist * mask, so masked-out zeros join it; with large distances every
    negative weight then underflows and closest_negative is ~0. masked_max=True (CAJ_fix) uses valid entries only,
    and sets masked entries to -inf before exp so they cannot overflow."""
    if masked_max:
        valid = dist.masked_fill(mask == 0, float("-inf"))
        diff = valid - valid.max(dim=1, keepdim=True)[0]
    else:
        diff = dist - torch.max(dist * mask, dim=1, keepdim=True)[0]
    z = torch.sum(torch.exp(diff) * mask, dim=1, keepdim=True) + 1e-6
    return torch.exp(diff) * mask / z


def weighted_extremes(features, labels, alpha=1.0, masked_max=False):
    """Softmax-weighted furthest positive / closest negative per anchor (self-match included, as upstream)."""
    dist = pairwise_distance(features)
    same = labels[:, None].eq(labels[None, :]).float()
    dist_ap, dist_an = dist * same, dist * (1 - same)
    furthest_positive = (dist_ap * softmax_weights(dist_ap * alpha, same, masked_max)).sum(1)
    closest_negative = (dist_an * softmax_weights(-dist_an * alpha, 1 - same, masked_max)).sum(1)
    return furthest_positive, closest_negative
In [14]:
# Pre-BN features with norm about 50, as in the collapsed run: the upstream weighting returns a closest-negative
# distance of about 0, so ADP sees no negatives; the corrected weighting returns the real distance.
torch.manual_seed(0)
features = F.normalize(torch.randn(64, 2048), dim=1) * 50
features_labels = torch.arange(16).repeat_interleave(4)
rows = []
for masked, name in ((False, "authors' code"), (True, "corrected (masked max)")):
    positive, negative = weighted_extremes(features, features_labels, masked_max=masked)
    rows.append([name, f"{positive.mean().item():.2f}", f"{negative.mean().item():.4f}"])
show_table(["Weighting", "Mean furthest-positive distance", "Mean closest-negative distance"], rows)
Weighting Mean furthest-positive distance Mean closest-negative distance

M0_CA is 1.45 mAP and 2.0 Rank-1 points above M0, higher on every seed (+1.47, +2.20, +0.67 mAP) and on 28 of 30 seed–gallery pairs. The gain is about three times M0's seed standard deviation (0.46 mAP) and holds across the CMC curve. M0_CA is also 2.3 mAP above the corrected CAJ, so channel augmentation adds to PMT rather than only bringing PMT to the CNN's level. This satisfies the rule fixed before the result, and M0_CA became the final candidate. No other configuration in Sections 5.4–5.5 met a comparable standard.

6. Discussion¶

6.1 Baselines and channel augmentation¶

PMT's components give a small but consistent gain: over three seeds M0 is above the plain ViT (V0) on all 30 seed–gallery pairs, and above the CNN baseline AGW by about 4 mAP points at roughly 3.6 times the computation. The corrected CAJ comes close to M0 with a ResNet-50 but is 0.8 mAP lower over three seeds; its single-seed tie with M0 did not hold, which is why every comparison in this notebook uses three seeds.

Channel augmentation is the one change that clearly improves PMT on validation (+1.45 mAP, all seeds). PMT already narrows the modality gap with a greyscale stage; copying a single colour channel to all three keeps varying the colour statistics throughout training, which appears to be a stronger version of the same idea. This also bears on RQ1: a smoother greyscale schedule did not help (Section 5.4), while stronger, persistent colour perturbation did.

The CAJ run shows that published code can be numerically fragile outside its original setting. A masking detail that is harmless for AGW's loss made CAJ's loss collapse the features, and only the training curve and a pilot evaluation exposed it. Correcting that one detail raised CAJ from 7.0% to 33.1% Rank-1 (seed 17). We therefore evaluated a short pilot before every full run and inspected each loss term rather than the total alone.

6.3 Limitations¶

  • Training identities, camera coverage (cam3 queries against cam4/5 galleries only on validation) and test-time settings differ from the published setting, so published benchmark scores should not be compared directly with these numbers.
  • Three training seeds bound the seed variation only roughly; differences below about one seed standard deviation (≈ 0.5 mAP for M0) are not treated as effects.
  • All results come from one dataset, and the candidate for the final stage changed after the configuration freeze (Section 4.8), although the decision rule was written before the deciding results.

The complete code (data interface, models, losses, training, feature export, evaluation and robustness tools), all run configurations and the tests are in project_code.zip, submitted together with this notebook. The core of each method is shown next to its description in Section 4. Datasets, checkpoints and exported features are not included.
